subtitle: From creation to Joseph in Egypt

sections.title: A Home Prepared for Humanity
sections.text: Genesis begins by telling us that Jehovah created the heavens and the earth. It then describes six creative days during which the earth was prepared for life. Light, dry land, vegetation, sea creatures, birds, and land animals all appear in the account. Finally, God creates humans in his image. Adam is formed from dust, and Eve is created as his companion. Jehovah places them in the garden of Eden, gives them meaningful work, and tells them they can eat from the trees except one. People were also given seed-bearing plants and fruit-bearing trees for food. Life begins with a beautiful purpose: fill the earth and care for it.
paragraphs: Genesis begins by telling us that Jehovah created the heavens and the earth. It then describes six creative days during which the earth was prepared for life. Light, dry land, vegetation, sea creatures, birds, and land animals all appear in the account. Finally, God creates humans in his image. Adam is formed from dust, and Eve is created as his companion. Jehovah places them in the garden of Eden, gives them meaningful work, and tells them they can eat from the trees except one. People were also given seed-bearing plants and fruit-bearing trees for food. Life begins with a beautiful purpose: fill the earth and care for it.

Here's an important detail: humans were given every seed-bearing plant and trees with seed-bearing fruit for food. The forbidden tree in Eden was one specific exception. Adam also had the enjoyable job of naming animals. Jehovah didn't create people for a life of boredom—he gave them a wonderful home, family, and work worth doing.
sections.takeaway: Jehovah created a beautiful home and gave humans a meaningful purpose.

sections.title: The Choice That Changed Everything
sections.text: A serpent questions Jehovah's direction and tells Eve that she won't die if she eats from the forbidden tree. Eve eats, and Adam joins her. Their choice brings sin, shame, and consequences for their family. But Jehovah doesn't abandon his purpose. In Genesis 3:15, he speaks of an offspring who will ultimately crush the serpent. Adam and Eve are sent out of Eden, and cherubs guard the way back. This is where the Bible first explains why humans suffer and die—and introduces a promise that runs through the rest of Scripture.
paragraphs: A serpent questions Jehovah's direction and tells Eve that she won't die if she eats from the forbidden tree. Eve eats, and Adam joins her. Their choice brings sin, shame, and consequences for their family. But Jehovah doesn't abandon his purpose. In Genesis 3:15, he speaks of an offspring who will ultimately crush the serpent. Adam and Eve are sent out of Eden, and cherubs guard the way back. This is where the Bible first explains why humans suffer and die—and introduces a promise that runs through the rest of Scripture.

Eve was deceived, while Adam also chose to disobey. When Jehovah questioned them, they hid and tried to shift responsibility. Outside Eden, life would now include pain, hard work, and death. Yet the promise of an offspring in Genesis 3:15 gave a glimpse of hope right from the start.
sections.takeaway: The choice in Eden changed human life, but Jehovah's promise gave hope.

sections.title: Two Brothers and a Growing Family
sections.text: Adam and Eve have children, including Cain and Abel. Abel seeks Jehovah's favor, but Cain grows angry and kills his brother despite a warning to control his feelings. Cain is sentenced to live as a wanderer. Genesis also records the growth of Cain's family and the birth of Seth, another son of Adam and Eve. Seth's line leads to faithful people such as Enoch, who walked with the true God. The family record reminds us that humans lived very long lives then, but sin and death still affected them. Adam himself eventually died.
paragraphs: Adam and Eve have children, including Cain and Abel. Abel seeks Jehovah's favor, but Cain grows angry and kills his brother despite a warning to control his feelings. Cain is sentenced to live as a wanderer. Genesis also records the growth of Cain's family and the birth of Seth, another son of Adam and Eve. Seth's line leads to faithful people such as Enoch, who walked with the true God. The family record reminds us that humans lived very long lives then, but sin and death still affected them. Adam himself eventually died.

Jehovah warned Cain that sin was crouching at the entrance and that he could get control over it. Sadly, Cain wouldn't listen. The family records in chapter 5 follow Adam's descendants, including Methuselah and Enoch, down toward Noah. The repeated words about people's deaths remind us of the terrible consequence of Eden.
sections.takeaway: Cain was warned about his anger. He still had a choice.

sections.title: A Violent World—and a Man Who Listened
sections.text: The world becomes filled with violence. Disobedient spirit sons of God take human wives, and their offspring, the Nephilim, are known for violence. Jehovah decides to bring a great Flood, but Noah is different: he walks with God. Jehovah tells him to build an ark and preserve his household along with representatives of the animals. Noah obeys. When the Flood comes, Noah, his wife, their three sons, and their sons' wives are safe inside. The account emphasizes both how serious the world's wickedness had become and how Jehovah protected those who listened to him.

Jehovah decides to bring a great Flood, but Noah is different: he walks with God. Jehovah tells him to build an ark and preserve his household along with representatives of the animals. Noah obeys. When the Flood comes, Noah, his wife, their three sons, and their sons' wives are safe inside. The account emphasizes both how serious the world's wickedness had become and how Jehovah protected those who listened to him.

Noah received detailed instructions for the ark and obeyed them. His family had to prepare food and preserve the animals Jehovah specified. When the time came, the family entered the ark and Jehovah shut the door. Rain fell for 40 days and nights. The floodwaters kept rising, and the world outside was swept away.
sections.takeaway: Noah showed his faith by acting on what Jehovah told him.

sections.title: Life Begins Again After the Flood
sections.text: The waters gradually go down. Noah sends out birds to learn whether dry land has appeared, and eventually his family leaves the ark. He offers sacrifices to Jehovah. God gives the family instructions about human life and the sacredness of blood. He also makes a covenant that a global flood will never again destroy all living creatures, using the rainbow as its sign. Genesis doesn't hide Noah's later family difficulties either. The closing part of this account includes Noah's words about his sons' descendants, showing that the story of humanity is already branching into new nations.

God gives the family instructions about human life and the sacredness of blood. He also makes a covenant that a global flood will never again destroy all living creatures, using the rainbow as its sign. Genesis doesn't hide Noah's later family difficulties either. The closing part of this account includes Noah's words about his sons' descendants, showing that the story of humanity is already branching into new nations.

Noah sent out a raven and then a dove to find out whether the land had dried. Later a dove returned with an olive leaf. When the family finally stepped outside, Noah made an offering to Jehovah. The rainbow covenant was reassuring, but chapter 9 also shows that even the family that survived the Flood could still make painful mistakes.
sections.takeaway: The rainbow was a reassuring sign of Jehovah's promise.

sections.title: Nations Spread Across the Earth
sections.text: Genesis traces families and nations descended from Noah's sons. Among the names is Nimrod, who comes to be associated with powerful cities and opposition to Jehovah. Later, people settle together and begin building a city and a tower at Babel. Instead of letting them succeed in resisting his direction to spread out, Jehovah confuses their language. Unable to understand one another, they scatter. The family record then narrows to Shem's descendants and leads us to Abram. His father Terah's household leaves Ur and eventually settles in Haran. A new part of the Bible's story is about to begin.
paragraphs: Genesis traces families and nations descended from Noah's sons. Among the names is Nimrod, who comes to be associated with powerful cities and opposition to Jehovah. Later, people settle together and begin building a city and a tower at Babel. Instead of letting them succeed in resisting his direction to spread out, Jehovah confuses their language. Unable to understand one another, they scatter. The family record then narrows to Shem's descendants and leads us to Abram. His father Terah's household leaves Ur and eventually settles in Haran. A new part of the Bible's story is about to begin.

Genesis 10 may seem like a long list of names, but those families became the peoples mentioned later in the Bible. At Babel, human pride led to a building project meant to make a name for its builders. Jehovah confused their language, scattering them. The record then traces Shem's line to Abram, through his father Terah.
sections.takeaway: These family records connect Noah's world to Abraham's.

sections.title: Abram Leaves the Familiar Behind
sections.text: Jehovah asks Abram to leave his home and go to a land that will be shown to him. Abram trusts the promise that his descendants will become a great nation and that families of the earth will benefit through him. He travels into Canaan with Sarai and Lot. A famine later takes them to Egypt, where Abram's fear creates trouble over Sarai's identity, but she is protected. After they return, their households have grown too large to remain together. Abram generously lets Lot choose where to settle. Lot chooses the well-watered district near Sodom, while Jehovah repeats his promise concerning the land.
paragraphs: Jehovah asks Abram to leave his home and go to a land that will be shown to him. Abram trusts the promise that his descendants will become a great nation and that families of the earth will benefit through him. He travels into Canaan with Sarai and Lot. A famine later takes them to Egypt, where Abram's fear creates trouble over Sarai's identity, but she is protected. After they return, their households have grown too large to remain together. Abram generously lets Lot choose where to settle. Lot chooses the well-watered district near Sodom, while Jehovah repeats his promise concerning the land.

Abram was 75 when he left Haran. He traveled to Canaan, built altars, and continued worshipping Jehovah. A famine brought trouble in Egypt, but afterward his household prospered. When his workers and Lot's workers quarreled, Abram let Lot choose where to live. Lot chose the fertile area near Sodom; Abram chose peace over arguing.
sections.takeaway: Abram trusted Jehovah and generously let Lot choose first.

sections.title: Lot Is Rescued, and a Promise Is Confirmed
sections.text: War breaks out between groups of kings, and Lot is captured. Abram gathers men from his household, rescues Lot, and recovers the people and belongings taken away. Afterward, Melchizedek, the king of Salem and priest of the Most High God, blesses Abram. Jehovah again assures Abram that he will have descendants, even though Abram still has no son by Sarai. God compares their number to the stars and makes a covenant about the land. He also foretells that Abram's descendants will suffer affliction in a foreign land before being delivered.
paragraphs: War breaks out between groups of kings, and Lot is captured. Abram gathers men from his household, rescues Lot, and recovers the people and belongings taken away. Afterward, Melchizedek, the king of Salem and priest of the Most High God, blesses Abram. Jehovah again assures Abram that he will have descendants, even though Abram still has no son by Sarai. God compares their number to the stars and makes a covenant about the land. He also foretells that Abram's descendants will suffer affliction in a foreign land before being delivered.

Abram didn't let the king of Sodom make him rich after rescuing Lot. Later, when he wondered how his promise of descendants could come true, Jehovah compared them to the stars. Abram put faith in Jehovah. The covenant also foretold hardship for his descendants in a foreign country before their eventual return.
sections.takeaway: Even faithful Abram wondered how Jehovah's promise would come true.

sections.title: Hagar, Ishmael, and the Promised Son
sections.text: Sarai has not yet borne a child, so she gives her servant Hagar to Abram as a secondary wife. Hagar becomes pregnant with Ishmael, and serious tension follows. Jehovah's angel comforts Hagar. Years later Jehovah makes his covenant with Abram more explicit, changes his name to Abraham and Sarai's name to Sarah, and introduces circumcision as a sign of the covenant. Then comes surprising news: Sarah herself will have a son, Isaac. Abraham already loves Ishmael, but Jehovah explains that the promised covenant will continue through Isaac.
paragraphs: Sarai has not yet borne a child, so she gives her servant Hagar to Abram as a secondary wife. Hagar becomes pregnant with Ishmael, and serious tension follows. Jehovah's angel comforts Hagar. Years later Jehovah makes his covenant with Abram more explicit, changes his name to Abraham and Sarai's name to Sarah, and introduces circumcision as a sign of the covenant. Then comes surprising news: Sarah herself will have a son, Isaac. Abraham already loves Ishmael, but Jehovah explains that the promised covenant will continue through Isaac.

Hagar fled during painful conflict, but Jehovah's angel met her near a spring and gave her reassurance. Later Jehovah changed Abram's name to Abraham and Sarai's to Sarah. He introduced circumcision as a covenant sign. Isaac would be born to Sarah, even though the family had been waiting for many years.
sections.takeaway: Jehovah noticed Hagar's distress and kept his promise to Abraham.

sections.title: Visitors, a Promise, and Judgment on Sodom
sections.text: Three visitors arrive at Abraham's tent. They bring word that Sarah will have a son, and she laughs because of her age. Abraham also learns that judgment is coming upon Sodom and pleads for the righteous. Angels visit Lot and hurry him and his family out of the city. Sodom and Gomorrah are destroyed, but Lot and his daughters survive. His wife looks back against the warning and loses her life. Genesis also records the troubled events involving Lot's daughters that lead to the family lines of Moab and Ammon. These chapters don't hide the difficult parts of human history.

Sodom and Gomorrah are destroyed, but Lot and his daughters survive. His wife looks back against the warning and loses her life. Genesis also records the troubled events involving Lot's daughters that lead to the family lines of Moab and Ammon. These chapters don't hide the difficult parts of human history.

Abraham asked whether the righteous would be destroyed along with the wicked in Sodom. In that city, Lot welcomed the visitors, who were angels, and they protected him from a violent crowd. Lot's family had to leave urgently. His wife's disobedience cost her life. The disturbing events involving Lot's daughters help explain the later nations of Moab and Ammon.
sections.takeaway: Abraham cared deeply about justice and innocent lives.

sections.title: At Last, Isaac Is Born
sections.text: Abraham and Sarah face another dangerous situation when Abraham describes her as his sister to King Abimelech. Jehovah intervenes to protect Sarah. Then the promised son finally arrives! Sarah gives birth to Isaac, and the family celebrates. But tension involving Ishmael leads to Hagar and Ishmael being sent away. Jehovah hears the boy and provides help in the wilderness, promising that he too will become a nation. Later Abraham settles a dispute with Abimelech over a well, making an agreement at Beer-sheba. Jehovah's promise through Isaac is moving forward.
paragraphs: Abraham and Sarah face another dangerous situation when Abraham describes her as his sister to King Abimelech. Jehovah intervenes to protect Sarah. Then the promised son finally arrives! Sarah gives birth to Isaac, and the family celebrates. But tension involving Ishmael leads to Hagar and Ishmael being sent away. Jehovah hears the boy and provides help in the wilderness, promising that he too will become a nation. Later Abraham settles a dispute with Abimelech over a well, making an agreement at Beer-sheba. Jehovah's promise through Isaac is moving forward.

Sarah's joy at Isaac's birth came after such a long wait! But serious tension involving Ishmael eventually led to Hagar and her son leaving. Jehovah heard the boy in the wilderness and helped them find water. Ishmael also received a promise of descendants, even though the special covenant would continue through Isaac.
sections.takeaway: After years of waiting, Sarah finally held Isaac in her arms!

sections.title: Abraham's Great Test
sections.text: Jehovah tests Abraham by directing him to offer Isaac. Abraham obeys, but at the decisive moment an angel stops him. A ram is provided instead, and Jehovah repeats the promise that blessings will come through Abraham's offspring. Later Sarah dies, and Abraham purchases a burial site in Canaan, the cave of Machpelah. These chapters show Abraham's strong faith, but they also contain the ordinary sorrow of losing someone he loved. The family has a place in the land Jehovah promised, even though the full inheritance still lies ahead.

A ram is provided instead, and Jehovah repeats the promise that blessings will come through Abraham's offspring. Later Sarah dies, and Abraham purchases a burial site in Canaan, the cave of Machpelah. These chapters show Abraham's strong faith, but they also contain the ordinary sorrow of losing someone he loved. The family has a place in the land Jehovah promised, even though the full inheritance still lies ahead.

The angel stopped Abraham before he sacrificed Isaac, and a ram was offered instead. Jehovah repeated the promise of blessings through Abraham's offspring. Then the account turns to sorrow: Sarah died at the age of 127. Abraham carefully arranged to purchase a burial place in Canaan, the land Jehovah had promised his family.
sections.takeaway: Abraham's faith remained strong during testing and family loss.

sections.title: A Wife for Isaac—and Two Very Different Twins
sections.text: Abraham sends a trusted servant to find a wife for Isaac among his relatives. At a well, Rebekah generously gives water to the servant and his camels. The servant sees how the request for guidance is answered, and Rebekah willingly travels to marry Isaac. Abraham later dies. Isaac and Rebekah eventually have twins, Esau and Jacob. Esau is born first, but he treats his birthright lightly, trading it to Jacob for a meal. What the brothers value—and the decisions they make—will affect their family for years.

The servant sees how the request for guidance is answered, and Rebekah willingly travels to marry Isaac. Abraham later dies. Isaac and Rebekah eventually have twins, Esau and Jacob. Esau is born first, but he treats his birthright lightly, trading it to Jacob for a meal. What the brothers value—and the decisions they make—will affect their family for years.

Rebekah willingly left her family to marry Isaac. They eventually had twins after Isaac prayed about their childlessness. Before their birth, Jehovah said two nations would come from them. Later Esau returned hungry from the field and sold his firstborn rights to Jacob for food. That hasty decision revealed how little he valued his birthright.
sections.takeaway: Our everyday choices often reveal what we value most.

sections.title: Isaac's Wells and Jacob's Blessing
sections.text: Jehovah confirms his promises to Isaac. Even as Isaac faces opposition and disputes over wells, he keeps moving rather than constantly fighting. His family story becomes more complicated when the time comes for Isaac to bless his sons. Rebekah helps Jacob present himself as Esau, and Jacob receives the blessing that Isaac had intended for his older son. Esau is furious and plans revenge. Jacob will have to leave home. Genesis shows how personal decisions, family favoritism, and God's larger purpose become tangled in this household.
paragraphs: Jehovah confirms his promises to Isaac. Even as Isaac faces opposition and disputes over wells, he keeps moving rather than constantly fighting. His family story becomes more complicated when the time comes for Isaac to bless his sons. Rebekah helps Jacob present himself as Esau, and Jacob receives the blessing that Isaac had intended for his older son. Esau is furious and plans revenge. Jacob will have to leave home. Genesis shows how personal decisions, family favoritism, and God's larger purpose become tangled in this household.

A famine led Isaac to Gerar, where Jehovah repeated his promises. Isaac avoided long disputes over wells by moving on until there was room for his household. Later Jacob received his father's blessing while disguised as Esau. This deception angered Esau so much that Jacob had to leave for safety.
sections.takeaway: God's promise continued despite this family's mistakes.

sections.title: A Dream at Bethel and a New Household
sections.text: Jacob travels toward his relatives. Along the way he dreams of a stairway reaching toward heaven, with angels moving on it. Jehovah repeats his promise about the land and Jacob's descendants. Jacob names the place Bethel. Later he meets Rachel and agrees to work for her father, Laban, for seven years so he can marry her. But Laban deceives Jacob into marrying Leah first. Jacob later marries Rachel too and continues working. The family line of Israel grows through a household marked by affection, rivalry, and hardship.

But Laban deceives Jacob into marrying Leah first. Jacob later marries Rachel too and continues working. The family line of Israel grows through a household marked by affection, rivalry, and hardship.

On his journey Jacob dreamed of a stairway reaching heaven with angels moving on it. Jehovah promised to be with him. Later Laban deceived Jacob into marrying Leah before Rachel. Leah's longing for affection and the rivalry between the sisters make it clear that this wasn't an easy household. Judah was among the sons born during these years.
sections.takeaway: Jehovah stayed with Jacob through uncertainty and unfair treatment.

sections.title: Jacob's Family Grows
sections.text: Jacob's children are born through Leah, Rachel, and their two servants, Bilhah and Zilpah. The account names sons who will become the ancestors of Israel's tribes, and it also mentions Jacob's daughter Dinah. Rachel eventually gives birth to Joseph. Jacob's flocks increase, but life with Laban becomes difficult. Jacob leaves with his family, and Laban follows. After a tense confrontation, the two make an agreement and set up a boundary marker. Jacob is heading back toward Canaan with a large household—but he still has to face his brother Esau.
paragraphs: Jacob's children are born through Leah, Rachel, and their two servants, Bilhah and Zilpah. Jacob is heading back toward Canaan with a large household—but he still has to face his brother Esau.

Rachel eventually gave birth to Joseph. Jacob's household and flocks grew, but Laban repeatedly made life difficult and changed his wages. When Jacob left, Rachel secretly took her father's household gods. Laban pursued them, and after a tense confrontation the two men agreed to respect a boundary between them.
sections.takeaway: Family tensions didn't stop Jehovah's purpose from moving forward.

sections.title: Jacob Becomes Israel
sections.text: As Jacob prepares to meet Esau, he worries that his brother may still want revenge. During the night Jacob wrestles with an angel and refuses to let go without a blessing. He receives a new name: Israel. The next day Jacob approaches Esau humbly. Instead of the attack Jacob fears, the brothers embrace and make peace. They eventually go their separate ways. It's a memorable turn in a family story that began with anger, deception, and a threatened life. Jacob continues his journey into Canaan.
paragraphs: As Jacob prepares to meet Esau, he worries that his brother may still want revenge. During the night Jacob wrestles with an angel and refuses to let go without a blessing. He receives a new name: Israel. The next day Jacob approaches Esau humbly. Instead of the attack Jacob fears, the brothers embrace and make peace. They eventually go their separate ways. It's a memorable turn in a family story that began with anger, deception, and a threatened life. Jacob continues his journey into Canaan.

Jacob sent gifts ahead and divided his camp because he feared an attack. He prayed to Jehovah, remembering the help he'd already received. After wrestling through the night with an angel, he received the name Israel. Then came a surprise: Esau ran toward Jacob, embraced him, and both brothers wept. Their meeting ended peacefully.
sections.takeaway: The brothers' reunion went differently from what Jacob feared.

sections.title: Painful Family Events and New Beginnings
sections.text: At Shechem, Dinah is sexually assaulted. Her brothers Simeon and Levi respond with a deceitful and violent attack on the men of the city. Jehovah then directs Jacob to return to Bethel, and Jacob tells his household to remove foreign gods. More family changes follow: Rachel dies while giving birth to Benjamin, and Isaac later dies. Genesis also records Esau's descendants and the rulers associated with Edom. Not every chapter is a dramatic adventure, but these accounts help explain the peoples and family lines that appear later in the Bible.

Jehovah then directs Jacob to return to Bethel, and Jacob tells his household to remove foreign gods. More family changes follow: Rachel dies while giving birth to Benjamin, and Isaac later dies. Genesis also records Esau's descendants and the rulers associated with Edom. Not every chapter is a dramatic adventure, but these accounts help explain the peoples and family lines that appear later in the Bible.

Chapter 34 records Dinah's assault and her brothers' violent revenge. Later Jacob removed foreign gods from his household and returned to Bethel. Rachel died giving birth to Benjamin; the account also mentions Reuben's wrongdoing with Bilhah. Isaac later died, and Esau and Jacob buried him. Esau's descendants, the Edomites, receive their own family record.
sections.takeaway: These difficult family events explain much of Israel's later history.

sections.title: Joseph's Dreams—and His Brothers' Betrayal
sections.text: Jacob favors Joseph, and Joseph's dreams suggest that his family will one day bow before him. His brothers become bitterly jealous. They sell him to traders heading for Egypt and deceive Jacob into thinking Joseph has died. The story then briefly follows Judah and Tamar. After Judah fails to arrange the marriage that Tamar had been promised, she takes unusual action that exposes his wrongdoing. She bears twins, Perez and Zerah. That family line will matter later. Meanwhile Joseph has been taken far from home, but his story is far from over.
paragraphs: Jacob favors Joseph, and Joseph's dreams suggest that his family will one day bow before him. His brothers become bitterly jealous. They sell him to traders heading for Egypt and deceive Jacob into thinking Joseph has died. The story then briefly follows Judah and Tamar. After Judah fails to arrange the marriage that Tamar had been promised, she takes unusual action that exposes his wrongdoing. She bears twins, Perez and Zerah. That family line will matter later. Meanwhile Joseph has been taken far from home, but his story is far from over.

Reuben originally wanted to save Joseph, but the brothers sold him and used his special garment to make Jacob believe he was dead. Chapter 38 then turns to Judah and Tamar. Judah eventually admitted his own wrongdoing. Tamar's twin sons, Perez and Zerah, became important names in the family history that followed.
sections.takeaway: Joseph's brothers tried to end his story. They couldn't.

sections.title: From Prison to Pharaoh's Court
sections.text: In Egypt, Joseph serves in Potiphar's house and earns trust. When Potiphar's wife repeatedly tries to seduce him, Joseph refuses. She falsely accuses him, and he is sent to prison. There he helps interpret the dreams of two prisoners. Later Pharaoh has disturbing dreams, and Joseph explains that Egypt will have seven years of abundance followed by seven years of famine. Pharaoh appoints him to supervise food storage and distribution. Joseph rises from prison to become a powerful administrator, while keeping his confidence in Jehovah.
paragraphs: In Egypt, Joseph serves in Potiphar's house and earns trust. When Potiphar's wife repeatedly tries to seduce him, Joseph refuses. She falsely accuses him, and he is sent to prison. There he helps interpret the dreams of two prisoners. Later Pharaoh has disturbing dreams, and Joseph explains that Egypt will have seven years of abundance followed by seven years of famine. Pharaoh appoints him to supervise food storage and distribution. Joseph rises from prison to become a powerful administrator, while keeping his confidence in Jehovah.

Joseph explained the dreams of Pharaoh's cupbearer and baker while he was imprisoned. The cupbearer forgot about him until Pharaoh had dreams nobody could explain. Joseph credited God for the interpretation, advised saving food, and was put in charge of preparations. His sons Manasseh and Ephraim were born before the famine.
sections.takeaway: Joseph remained faithful whether he was a servant, prisoner, or ruler.

sections.title: The Brothers Face a Test
sections.text: Famine brings Joseph's brothers to Egypt to buy food. They bow before a ruler they don't recognize: Joseph himself. He remembers his dreams but doesn't immediately reveal who he is. Instead he tests them, watching how they treat one another and their youngest brother, Benjamin. They return with Benjamin, and a silver cup is found in Benjamin's bag as part of Joseph's test. Judah offers himself in Benjamin's place rather than bring more grief to their father. Joseph can see that the brothers' attitude has changed.
paragraphs: Famine brings Joseph's brothers to Egypt to buy food. They bow before a ruler they don't recognize: Joseph himself. He remembers his dreams but doesn't immediately reveal who he is. Instead he tests them, watching how they treat one another and their youngest brother, Benjamin. They return with Benjamin, and a silver cup is found in Benjamin's bag as part of Joseph's test. Judah offers himself in Benjamin's place rather than bring more grief to their father. Joseph can see that the brothers' attitude has changed.

Joseph kept Simeon behind and required the brothers to return with Benjamin. Their father Jacob was afraid of losing another son. When the brothers returned, Joseph arranged for his silver cup to be found in Benjamin's bag. Judah offered to take Benjamin's place rather than break his father's heart. Joseph could see their attitude had changed.
sections.takeaway: The brothers showed change by protecting Benjamin.

sections.title: A Family Reunited in Egypt
sections.text: Joseph can no longer hold back his emotions. He tells his brothers who he is, forgives them, and explains that God has used the situation to preserve life during the famine. Pharaoh invites the family to move to Egypt. Jacob travels there and finally sees Joseph again, and the family settles in Goshen. Jacob even meets Pharaoh. As the famine continues, Joseph manages Egypt's food supply. This move protects Jacob's family for the moment, but it also explains how their descendants come to be living in Egypt when Exodus begins.
paragraphs: Joseph can no longer hold back his emotions. He tells his brothers who he is, forgives them, and explains that God has used the situation to preserve life during the famine. Pharaoh invites the family to move to Egypt. Jacob travels there and finally sees Joseph again, and the family settles in Goshen. Jacob even meets Pharaoh. As the famine continues, Joseph manages Egypt's food supply. This move protects Jacob's family for the moment, but it also explains how their descendants come to be living in Egypt when Exodus begins.

Joseph's brothers were stunned when he revealed his identity. After he reassured them, they returned to tell Jacob that Joseph was alive. The whole household traveled to Egypt, and Jacob had a deeply emotional reunion with his son in Goshen. Pharaoh welcomed the family, while Joseph continued managing Egypt's food supplies during the famine.
sections.takeaway: After years of sorrow, Joseph and Jacob saw each other again!

sections.title: Final Blessings and a Promise for the Future
sections.text: Near the end of his life, Jacob blesses Joseph's two sons, giving special priority to the younger Ephraim. He then speaks prophetic words over his own sons, including an important promise connected with Judah. Jacob dies and is buried in Canaan. Joseph's brothers fear that he might now seek revenge, but he assures them of his forgiveness. Joseph himself lives to old age and, before dying, expresses confidence that God will bring the family out of Egypt. He asks that his bones be taken along when that day comes. Genesis ends with the family waiting for God's promises to unfold.
paragraphs: Near the end of his life, Jacob blesses Joseph's two sons, giving special priority to the younger Ephraim. He then speaks prophetic words over his own sons, including an important promise connected with Judah. Jacob dies and is buried in Canaan. Joseph's brothers fear that he might now seek revenge, but he assures them of his forgiveness. Joseph himself lives to old age and, before dying, expresses confidence that God will bring the family out of Egypt. He asks that his bones be taken along when that day comes. Genesis ends with the family waiting for God's promises to unfold.

Jacob gave special blessings to Joseph's sons Ephraim and Manasseh. His words about Judah pointed ahead to the one called Shiloh. After Jacob died, his sons buried him in Canaan. Joseph's brothers feared revenge, but he comforted them and promised to care for their families. Before his own death, Joseph expressed confidence in Jehovah's promise to bring them back.
sections.takeaway: Genesis ends with Jehovah's promises still unfolding.
